lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 6, which Chinese dynasty painted misty mountain scrolls? (The Song dynasty.) Today: art made from 1450 to 1750 in India, Japan and the Ottoman Empire.
The Mughal emperors ruled much of India from 1526. Akbar (1542-1605) set up workshops where many artists made one painting together: one drew it, others coloured it, and a master painted the faces.

Mughal miniatures are small and bright, painted with very fine brushes, colours ground from minerals, and real gold. Scenes are seen from high up, with flat patterned carpets, and pages have borders of flowers.
Jahangir (1569-1627), Akbar's son, loved true-to-life paintings of birds, animals and flowers, and his artists painted them from life. His son Shah Jahan began the Taj Mahal in 1632.

In Japan, woodblock prints called ukiyo-e, pictures of the floating world, showed actors, city life, stories and later landscapes. Hishikawa Moronobu (1618-1694) made them popular; one design could print hundreds of copies.

A print was teamwork: the artist drew the design, a carver cut the wood blocks, a printer inked and printed them, and a publisher sold them. Look for bold outlines, flat colour, a title box (a cartouche) and a seal.

In the Ottoman Empire, potters in Iznik made glowing tiles, at their best from about 1550 to 1600: cobalt blue, turquoise, green and a raised bright red, with tulips, carnations and long curving saz leaves.
Try it in the world: design a square tile with a tulip, a carnation and a curving leaf in blue, turquoise and red. Then repeat it four times. Next: graphic design.

exercises.prompt: Who set up the Mughal emperors' painting workshops?
exercises.explain: Akbar (1542-1605) set up workshops where many artists worked together.

exercises.prompt: Mughal miniatures were often painted by teams, with one artist drawing and others colouring.
exercises.explain: True: several artists often worked on one painting.

exercises.hint: It is the name of Japanese prints of city life.
exercises.explain: Ukiyo-e means pictures of the floating world: the lively world of theatres and city life.

exercises.prompt: Match each art to where it was made.
exercises.hint: Mughal emperors ruled India; Iznik is a town in today's Turkey.
exercises.explain: Miniatures: India; ukiyo-e: Japan; Iznik tiles: the Ottoman Empire; porcelain: China.

exercises.prompt: Which flower is often painted on Iznik tiles?
exercises.hint: Look at the red flower on this tile.
exercises.explain: Tulips, with carnations and curving saz leaves.

exercises.hint: The tulip stands up in red; the carnation is a fan of petals; the saz leaf is long and curved.
exercises.explain: The red tulip at the top, the carnation's fan of petals, the long curving saz leaf, and the blue border round the edge.

exercises.hint: The border is the decorated frame; the sky is gold; the pavilion is the building; the pool is the water.
exercises.explain: The flowered border round the page, the gold sky at the top, the pavilion with the ruler, and the pool in the garden.

exercises.prompt: Which colours are typical of Iznik tiles?
choices: cobalt blue, turquoise, green and red
exercises.explain: Cobalt blue, turquoise, green and a bright raised red on white.

exercises.prompt: Who cut the design into the wood blocks for a Japanese print?
exercises.hint: A print took a team of four.
exercises.explain: The artist drew it, a carver cut it, a printer printed it and a publisher sold it.

exercises.prompt: Iznik potters were inspired by Chinese blue-and-white porcelain.
exercises.explain: True: Chinese porcelain was treasured in Istanbul, and Iznik potters took up its blue and white.

exercises.prompt: How do Mughal paintings show a garden?
exercises.hint: Look at the carpets and the pool.
choices: from high up, with flat patterns
exercises.explain: From a high viewpoint, with flat bright patterns, not one-point perspective.

exercises.prompt: What did Jahangir most like his artists to paint?
choices: birds, animals and flowers, from life

exercises.prompt: The Blue Mosque in Istanbul was finished in 1616, and work on the Taj Mahal began in 1632. How many years apart are they?
exercises.hint: Take the earlier year from the later one.
The cartouche is the title box; the seal is the small red stamp.
exercises.explain: The title box (cartouche) top right, the red seal, the patterned kimono and the umbrella.

exercises.prompt: Put these in time order, the earliest first.
items: work begins on the Taj Mahal

exercises.prompt: Why do tulips and blue-and-white patterns turn up in China, Turkey and Europe?
exercises.hint: How did porcelain and tiles reach other countries?
exercises.explain: Traders carried pots, tiles and cloth across Asia and Europe, and artists copied what they admired.

exercises.prompt: Sort the art by how it was made.
exercises.hint: Woodblocks print; brushes paint; tiles and porcelain go in a kiln.
exercises.explain: Ukiyo-e were printed from carved woodblocks onto paper. Mughal miniatures were painted with fine brushes on paper. Iznik tiles and Chinese porcelain are clay, glazed and fired in a kiln.
